title: Enron – from “perpetual innovation” to bankruptcy (Session 4)
text: Enron, a Houston energy company, turned from gas pipelines into a trader of gas, electricity, broadband capacity, paper and much else. Business writers praised its capacity for “perpetual innovation”, and for years it ranked among the most innovative companies and the best employers in the US.

Artifacts seen in the class material: a glass tower, the tilted “crooked E” logo, a huge trading floor, very large bonuses, special-purpose vehicles named after Star Wars characters. Its official values were Respect, Integrity, Communication and Excellence.

Employees were ranked every year and the bottom 15 % were fired (“rank and yank”). Profits were booked with mark-to-market accounting (expected future profits recorded today) and debt was parked off the balance sheet. The share price peaked at about $90 in August 2000.
In 2001 the CEO resigned, hidden losses and debts came out and the SEC opened an investigation; Enron filed for bankruptcy on 2 December 2001 and its auditor Arthur Andersen collapsed with it.
